0.title: median()
0.text: The median method returns the median value of a given key. The median is the middle value when all values are sorted in order. For collections with an even number of items, it returns the average of the two middle values. collect1, 3, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9 .median //  6 For an even count, it returns the average of two middle values: collect1, 2, 3, 4 .median //  2.5 By property: collect { name: 'Desk', price: 200 }, { name: 'Chair', price: 100 }, { name: 'Lamp', price: 50 }, .median'price' //  100 For

1.title: mode()
1.text: The mode method returns the mode value of a given key, which is the value that appears most frequently in the collection. If multiple values share the highest frequency, all of them are returned. Returns null if the collection is empty. collect1, 1, 2, 4 .mode //  1 For multiple modes, all are returned: collect1, 1, 2, 2, 3 .mode //  1, 2 By property: collect { name: 'Desk', category: 'furniture' }, { name: 'Chair', category: 'furniture' }, { name: 'Laptop', category: 'electronics' }, .mode'cat

2.title: count()
2.text: The count method returns the total number of items in the collection. collect1, 2, 3 .count //  3 For Count items grouped by key/callback, use countBy. For Check if collection has no items, use isEmpty.

3.title: sum()
3.text: Sum all items, or a specific key/callback result. collect1, 2, 3 .sum //  6 To sum a property: collect { id: 1, total: 100 }, { id: 2, total: 50 }, .sum'total' //  150 For Calculate average instead, use avg. For Get minimum value, use min.

4.title: avg()
4.text: The avg method returns the average value of a given key. collect1, 2, 3 .avg //  2 By property: collect { name: 'Desk', price: 200 }, { name: 'Chair', price: 100 }, .avg'price' //  150 For Get total instead of average, use sum. For Get minimum value, use min.

5.title: average()
5.text: The average method is an alias for the avg method. For Primary method, use avg.

6.title: min()
6.text: The min method returns the minimum value of a given key. collect3, 1, 2 .min //  1 By property: collect { name: 'Desk', price: 200 }, { name: 'Chair', price: 100 }, .min'price' //  100 For Get maximum value, use max. For Get average value, use avg.

7.title: max()
7.text: The max method returns the maximum value of a given key. collect1, 2, 3 .max //  3 By property: collect { name: 'Desk', price: 200 }, { name: 'Chair', price: 100 }, .max'price' //  200 For Get minimum value, use min. For Get average value, use avg.

8.title: percentage()
8.text: The percentage method may be used to quickly determine the percentage of items in the collection that pass a given truth test. collect1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3 .percentagevalue => value === 1 //  33.33 You may also specify precision: collect { name: 'Desk', available: true }, { name: 'Chair', available: true }, { name: 'Lamp', available: true }, { name: 'Rug', available: false }, .percentagep => p.available, 1 //  75.0 For Count total items, use count. For Get matching items, use filter.

9.title: implode()
9.text: The implode method joins items in a collection. Its arguments depend on the type of items in the collection. If the collection contains arrays or objects, pass the key of the attribute you wish to join, and the "glue" string. For simple values, pass just the glue string. For a simple array: collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5 .implode'-' //  '1-2-3-4-5' By property: collect { name: 'Desk' }, { name: 'Chair' }, { name: 'Bookcase' }, .implode'name', ', ' //  'Desk, Chair, Bookcase' You may also pass a callback:

10.title: join()
10.text: The join method joins the collection's values with a string. Using its second argument, you may also specify how the final element should be appended, which is useful for natural-language formatting like "and" or "or". collect'a', 'b', 'c' .join', ' //  'a, b, c' You may specify a final glue: collect'a', 'b', 'c' .join', ', ', and ' //  'a, b, and c' For Oxford comma style: collect'Taylor', 'Abigail', 'Dayle' .join', ', ', and ' //  'Taylor, Abigail, and Dayle' For Join by property or callback,

11.title: toString()
11.text: The toString method returns the collection as a comma-separated string. This method is automatically called when the collection is coerced to a string. collect1, 2, 3 .toString //  '1, 2, 3' For Join with custom separator, use join. For Join by property or callback, use implode.

12.title: reduce()
12.text: The reduce method reduces the collection to a single value, passing the result of each iteration into the subsequent iteration. The value for the accumulator on the first iteration is the initial value; on subsequent iterations, it is the value returned by the previous callback. collect1, 2, 3 .reducecarry, item => carry + item, 0 //  6 To build an object: collect { id: 1, name: 'Taylor' }, { id: 2, name: 'Abigail' }, .reducecarry, user => { carryuser.id = user.name return carry }, {} //  { 1:

13.title: reduceSpread()
13.text: The reduceSpread method reduces the collection to multiple values using spread arguments. The callback receives the accumulated values spread as individual arguments, followed by the current item and key. It must return an array of the same shape as the initial values. To track multiple values: collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5 .reduceSpreadsum, product, item => sum + item, product  item, 0, 1 //  15, 120 sum=15, product=120 For Reduce to a single value, use reduce. For Reduce by mutating an object, use red

14.title: reduceWithKeys()
14.text: The reduceWithKeys method reduces the collection with access to both value and key. This method works identically to reduce since the key is always provided as the third argument. It exists for API compatibility with Laravel. To build a keyed object: collect{ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 } .reduceWithKeyscarry, value, key => { carrykey = value  2 return carry }, {} //  { a: 2, b: 4, c: 6 } For Primary reduce method, use reduce.

15.title: reduceInto()
15.text: The reduceInto method reduces the collection into an existing object, mutating it. Unlike reduce, the callback does not return a value. Instead, it modifies the carry object directly. The same object is returned at the end. To build an object by mutation: collect1, 2, 3 .reduceInto{ total: 0 }, carry, item => { carry.total += item } //  { total: 6 } To populate an existing array: collect { name: 'Taylor', active: true }, { name: 'Abigail', active: true }, { name: 'James', active: false }, .redu

16.title: toArray()
16.text: The toArray method converts the collection into a plain array. For associative collections keyed objects, it returns a record instead. Nested collections are also recursively converted to arrays/records. collect1, 2, 3 .toArray //  1, 2, 3 For an associative collection: collect{ a: 1, b: 2 } .toArray //  { a: 1, b: 2 } For nested collections: collectcollect1, 2, collect3, 4 .toArray //  1, 2, 3, 4 For Get raw items without recursion, use all. For Get values as new collection, use values.

17.title: toJson()
17.text: The toJson method converts the collection into a JSON serialized string. collect{ name: 'Desk', price: 200 } .toJson //  '{"name":"Desk","price":200}' For JSON with indentation, use toPrettyJson. For Convert to array/record, use toArray.

18.title: toPrettyJson()

19.title: containsStrict()
19.text: The containsStrict method determines whether the collection contains a given item using strict comparison ===. Unlike contains which uses loose equality, this method distinguishes between types. For example, 1 and '1' are not equal under strict comparison. collect1, '1' .containsStrict1 //  true You may also use key/value with strict comparison: collect{ id: 1 }, { id: '1' } .containsStrict'id', 1 //  true first item matches, second does not For loose equality ==, use contains. For the inverse

20.title: doesntContain()
20.text: The doesntContain method determines whether the collection does not contain a given item. This method is the inverse of contains and uses loose equality == for comparison. It returns true when the item is NOT found in the collection. collect1, 2, 3 .doesntContain4 //  true You may also pass a callback: collect { name: 'Taylor', role: 'editor' }, { name: 'Abigail', role: 'editor' }, .doesntContainu => u.role === 'admin' //  true For the inverse true if found, use contains. For strict equality ==

21.title: doesntContainStrict()
21.text: The doesntContainStrict method determines whether the collection does not contain a given item using strict comparison ===. This method is the inverse of containsStrict and returns true when the item is NOT found. collect1, 2, 3 .doesntContainStrict'1' //  true string '1' is not strictly equal to number 1 For the inverse with strict equality, use containsStrict. For loose equality ==, use doesntContain.

22.title: has()
22.text: The has method determines if a given key exists in the collection. When an array of keys is passed, returns true only if ALL keys exist. For a single key: collect{ a: 1, b: 2 } .has'a' //  true For multiple keys all must exist: collect{ a: 1, b: 2 } .has'a', 'c' //  false c does not exist For checking if any key exists, use hasAny. For Check if a value exists, use contains.

23.title: hasAny()
23.text: The hasAny method determines if any of the given keys exist in the collection. Returns true if at least one of the provided keys exists. Returns false for empty collections regardless of the keys provided. collect{ a: 1, b: 2 } .hasAny'b', 'c', 'd' //  true b exists If no keys match: collect{ a: 1, b: 2 } .hasAny'c', 'd' //  false For checking if all keys exist, use has. For Check if a value exists, use contains.

24.title: isEmpty()
24.text: The isEmpty method returns true if the collection is empty. collect .isEmpty //  true For a non-empty collection: collect1, 2, 3 .isEmpty //  false For the inverse true if has items, use isNotEmpty. For Get the number of items, use count.

25.title: isNotEmpty()
25.text: The isNotEmpty method returns true if the collection is not empty. collect1, 2, 3 .isNotEmpty //  true For an empty collection: collect .isNotEmpty //  false For the inverse true if empty, use isEmpty. For Get the number of items, use count.

26.title: containsOneItem()
26.text: The containsOneItem method returns true if the collection contains exactly one item. When a callback is provided, returns true only if exactly one item passes the test. collect'a' .containsOneItem //  true You may also pass a callback: collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5 .containsOneItemn => n > 4 //  true only 5 passes For checking if more than one item, use hasMany. For Similar but throws if not exactly one, use hasSole.

27.title: hasMany()
27.text: The hasMany method returns true if the collection contains more than one item. When a callback or key/value pair is provided, returns true only if more than one item passes the test. collect1, 2, 3 .hasMany //  true You may also pass a callback: collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5 .hasManyn => n > 3 //  true 4 and 5 pass For checking if exactly one item, use containsOneItem. For checking if exactly one matching item, use hasSole.

28.title: hasSole()
28.text: The hasSole method returns true if the collection contains exactly one item that passes the given truth test. Unlike sole, this method returns a boolean instead of throwing an exception when zero or multiple items match. collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5 .hasSolen => n > 4 //  true only 5 passes For multiple matches: collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5 .hasSolen => n > 3 //  false 4 and 5 both pass For getting the item throws if not exactly one, use sole. For Check without filter, use containsOneItem.

29.title: every()
29.text: The every method verifies that all elements of the collection pass a given truth test. Returns true if the callback returns truthy for every item. If the collection is empty, every returns true vacuous truth. You may also pass a callback: collect1, 2, 3 .everyn => n < 10 //  true You may also pass a property key: collect{ active: true }, { active: true } .every'active' //  true Or use key/operator/value syntax: collect{ qty: 5 }, { qty: 10 } .every'qty', '>=', 5 //  true For checking if any ite

30.title: some()
30.text: The some method is an alias for the contains method. It determines whether the collection contains any items that pass the given truth test. This method is useful for developers coming from JavaScript's Array.some convention. collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5 .somen => n > 4 //  true For Primary method identical behavior, use contains. For checking if all items pass, use every.

31.title: offsetExists()
31.text: The offsetExists method determines if a key exists at the given offset. This method implements the ArrayAccess interface pattern, allowing bracket-style key existence checks. It is used internally for array-like access. collect{ a: 1, b: 2 } .offsetExists'a' //  true For Primary method for key existence checks, use has. For Get value at offset, use offsetGet.

32.title: zip()
32.text: The zip method merges together the values of the given array with the values of the original collection at their corresponding index. This is useful for pairing related data from multiple sources, such as names with scores or dates with values. To pair names with scores: collect'Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie' .zip85, 92, 78 //  'Alice', 85, 'Bob', 92, 'Charlie', 78 You may pass multiple arrays: collect1, 2, 3 .zip'a', 'b', 'c', true, false, true //  1, 'a', true, 2, 'b', false, 3, 'c', true For Use v

33.title: diff()
33.text: The diff method compares the collection against another array or collection based on its values. This method returns the values in the original collection that are not present in the given collection. collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5 .diff2, 4, 6 //  1, 3, 5 To find missing items: const required = 'name', 'email', 'phone' const provided = 'name', 'email' collectrequired.diffprovided //  'phone' For Get items present in both collections, use intersect. For comparing by keys instead of values, use diffKeys.

34.title: diffUsing()
34.text: The diffUsing method compares the collection against another array or collection using a callback. The callback should return 0 when two values are considered equal, a negative number when the first is less than the second, or a positive number otherwise. For case-insensitive comparison: collect'Apple', 'Banana' .diffUsing'apple', 'cherry', a, b => a.toLowerCase.localeCompareb.toLowerCase //  'Banana' For comparing using default equality, use diff. For comparing keys and values with a callback,

35.title: diffKeys()
35.text: The diffKeys method compares the collection against another array or collection based on its keys. This method returns the key/value pairs in the original collection whose keys are not present in the given collection. To find extra fields: collect{ name: 'Alice', age: 30, city: 'NYC' } .diffKeys{ name: '', age: 0 } //  { city: 'NYC' } For comparing by values instead of keys, use diff. For comparing by both keys and values, use diffAssoc.

36.title: diffKeysUsing()
36.text: The diffKeysUsing method compares the collection against another array or collection based on its keys using a callback. The callback should return 0 when two keys are considered equal. For case-insensitive key comparison: collect{ Name: 'Alice', AGE: 30 } .diffKeysUsing{ name: '', age: 0 }, a, b => a.toLowerCase.localeCompareb.toLowerCase //  {} all keys match case-insensitively For comparing keys using default equality, use diffKeys.

37.title: diffAssoc()
37.text: The diffAssoc method compares the collection against another array or collection based on both its keys and values. This method returns the key/value pairs in the original collection that are not present in the given collection. To compare key-value pairs: collect{ color: 'red', size: 'large', price: 100 } .diffAssoc{ color: 'red', size: 'medium' } //  { size: 'large', price: 100 } For comparing by values only, use diff. For comparing by keys only, use diffKeys.

38.title: diffAssocUsing()
38.text: The diffAssocUsing method compares the collection against another array or collection based on its keys and values, using a callback for key comparison. The callback should return 0 when two keys are considered equal. For case-insensitive key comparison: collect{ Name: 'Alice', Age: 30 } .diffAssocUsing{ name: 'Alice', age: 25 }, a, b => a.toLowerCase.localeCompareb.toLowerCase //  { Age: 30 } Name matches, Age differs in value For comparing using default key equality, use diffAssoc. For compar

39.title: intersect()
39.text: The intersect method removes any values from the original collection that are not present in the given array or collection. The resulting collection will preserve the original collection's keys. To find common elements: collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5 .intersect2, 4, 6, 8 //  2, 4 To check permissions: const userPermissions = 'read', 'write', 'delete' const required = 'read', 'admin' collectuserPermissions.intersectrequired //  'read' For Get items NOT present in the other collection, use diff. For Inters

40.title: intersectUsing()
40.text: The intersectUsing method removes values not present in the given array or collection, using a callback for comparison. The callback should return 0 when two values are considered equal. For case-insensitive intersection: collect'Apple', 'Banana', 'Cherry' .intersectUsing'apple', 'cherry', a, b => a.toLowerCase.localeCompareb.toLowerCase //  'Apple', 'Cherry' For Intersect using default equality, use intersect.

41.title: intersectAssoc()
41.text: The intersectAssoc method compares the collection against another array or collection, returning key/value pairs that are present in both. Unlike intersect, this method considers both keys and values when determining matches. To find matching key-value pairs: collect{ name: 'Alice', age: 30, city: 'NYC' } .intersectAssoc{ name: 'Alice', age: 25, city: 'NYC' } //  { name: 'Alice', city: 'NYC' } For Intersect by values only, use intersect. For Intersect by keys only, use intersectByKeys.

42.title: intersectAssocUsing()
42.text: The intersectAssocUsing method compares the collection against another array or collection based on both keys and values, using a callback for key comparison. The callback should return 0 when two keys are considered equal. For case-insensitive key matching: collect{ Name: 'Alice', AGE: 30 } .intersectAssocUsing{ name: 'Alice', age: 30 }, a, b => a.toLowerCase.localeCompareb.toLowerCase //  { Name: 'Alice', AGE: 30 } For Intersect using default key equality, use intersectAssoc.

43.title: intersectByKeys()
43.text: The intersectByKeys method removes any keys from the original collection that are not present in the given array or collection. This is useful for filtering an object to only include specific fields. To filter to allowed fields: collect{ name: 'Alice', age: 30, password: 'secret' } .intersectByKeys{ name: '', age: '' } //  { name: 'Alice', age: 30 } For Intersect by values instead of keys, use intersect. For Intersect by both keys and values, use intersectAssoc.

44.title: merge()
44.text: The merge method merges the given array or collection with the original collection. If a string key in the given items matches a string key in the original collection, the given item's value will overwrite the value in the original collection. To merge objects: collect{ name: 'Alice', age: 25 } .merge{ age: 30, city: 'NYC' } //  { name: 'Alice', age: 30, city: 'NYC' } For arrays, items are appended: collect1, 2 .merge3, 4 //  1, 2, 3, 4 For keeping original values for duplicate keys, use union.

45.title: mergeRecursive()
45.text: The mergeRecursive method merges the given array or collection recursively with the original collection. If a string key in the given items matches a string key in the original collection, the values for these keys are merged together into an object, and this is done recursively for nested structures. For recursive merge: collect{ user: { name: 'Alice', settings: { theme: 'dark' } } } .mergeRecursive{ user: { settings: { language: 'en' } } } //  { user: { name: 'Alice', settings: { theme: 'dark

46.title: union()
46.text: The union method adds the given array to the collection. If the given array contains keys that are already in the original collection, the original collection's values will be preferred. This is the opposite of merge which prefers new values. To prefer original values: collect{ a: 1, b: 2 } .union{ b: 3, c: 4 } //  { a: 1, b: 2, c: 4 } To fill in defaults: const userSettings = collectuser.settings .uniondefaultSettings // Original settings preserved, defaults fill gaps For preferring new values

47.title: combine()
47.text: The combine method combines the values of the collection, as keys, with the values of another array or collection. This is useful for creating key-value pairs from two separate lists. To create key-value mapping: collect'name', 'age', 'city' .combine'Alice', 30, 'NYC' //  { name: 'Alice', age: 30, city: 'NYC' } To build form data: collectfieldNames .combinefieldValues //  { field1: value1, field2: value2, ... } For Pair by index into nested arrays instead of key-value, use zip. For Extract key-

48.title: crossJoin()
48.text: The crossJoin method cross joins the collection's values among the given arrays or collections, returning a Cartesian product with all possible permutations. For a two-way cross join: collect'S', 'M', 'L' .crossJoin'red', 'blue' // //   'S', 'red', 'S', 'blue', //   'M', 'red', 'M', 'blue', //   'L', 'red', 'L', 'blue' // For a three-way cross join: collect1, 2 .crossJoin'a', 'b', true, false //  1, 'a', true, 1, 'a', false, 1, 'b', true, ... For Pair by index instead of creating all combinatio

49.title: concat()
49.text: The concat method appends the given array or collection's values onto the end of another collection. Unlike merge, this method does not consider keys and simply appends all values to the end. collect1, 2, 3 .concat4, 5, 6 //  1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 You may chain multiple concatenations: collect'a' .concat'b', 'c' .concat'd' //  'a', 'b', 'c', 'd' For Merge with key consideration, use merge. For Append single items mutates collection, use push.

50.title: put()
50.text: The put method sets the given key and value in the collection. If the key already exists, its value will be overwritten. This method mutates the collection. collect{ a: 1, b: 2 } .put'c', 3 .put'a', 10 //  { a: 10, b: 2, c: 3 } To build an object dynamically: collect{} .put'name', 'Alice' .put'age', 30 //  { name: 'Alice', age: 30 } For Append without specifying a key, use push. For Retrieve a value by key, use get.

51.title: push()
51.text: The push method appends one or more items to the end of the collection. This method mutates the collection and returns it for chaining. To append a single item: collect1, 2, 3 .push4 //  1, 2, 3, 4 To append multiple items: collect'a', 'b' .push'c', 'd', 'e' //  'a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e' For Add to the beginning, use prepend. For Set by key, use put.

52.title: prepend()
52.text: The prepend method adds an item to the beginning of the collection. You may optionally pass a second argument to set the key of the prepended item. This method mutates the collection. To prepend a value: collect2, 3, 4 .prepend1 //  1, 2, 3, 4 To prepend with a key: collect{ b: 2, c: 3 } .prepend1, 'a' //  { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 } For Add to the end, use push. For Prepend multiple values, use unshift.

53.title: unshift()
53.text: The unshift method is an alias for the prepend method, but accepts multiple values. It adds one or more items to the beginning of the collection, preserving their order. This method mutates the collection. To prepend multiple values: collect4, 5, 6 .unshift1, 2, 3 //  1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 For Add single item with optional key, use prepend. For Add to the end, use push.

54.title: add()
54.text: The add method is an alias for the push method. It appends a single item to the end of the collection. This method mutates the collection. To add an item: collect1, 2, 3 .add4 //  1, 2, 3, 4 For Primary method supports multiple items, use push.

55.title: multiply()
55.text: The multiply method creates multiple copies of all items in the collection. The resulting collection contains the original items repeated the specified number of times. To double the items: collect1, 2, 3 .multiply2 //  1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3 To repeat for display: collect'' .multiply5 .join'' //  '' For Pad to a specific size, use pad. For Generate a sequence of numbers, use range.

56.title: replace()
56.text: The replace method behaves similarly to merge; however, in addition to overwriting matching items that have string keys, the replace method will also overwrite items in the collection that have matching numeric keys. collect{ name: 'Alice', age: 25 } .replace{ age: 30, city: 'NYC' } //  { name: 'Alice', age: 30, city: 'NYC' } To replace array items by index: collect'a', 'b', 'c' .replace{ 1: 'B', 2: 'C' } //  'a', 'B', 'C' For Merge without replacing by numeric key, use merge. For Replace neste

57.title: replaceRecursive()
57.text: The replaceRecursive method works like replace, but it will recurse into nested objects and apply the same replacement process to the inner values. For recursive replacement: collect{ user: { name: 'Alice', settings: { theme: 'dark', lang: 'en' } } }.replaceRecursive{ user: { settings: { theme: 'light' } } } //  { user: { name: 'Alice', settings: { theme: 'light', lang: 'en' } } } For Shallow replacement, use replace. For Similar but merges arrays instead of replacing, use mergeRecursive.

58.title: with()
58.text: The with method joins the collection with a related collection, enabling operations that correlate items between the two. This is useful for scenarios similar to database joins where you need to work with related data sets. To join users with orders: const users = collect { id: 1, name: 'Taylor' }, { id: 2, name: 'Abigail' }, const orders = collect { userId: 1, total: 100 }, { userId: 1, total: 200 }, users.withorders.mapuser, related => { ...user, orderCount: related.count, } For Create cartes

59.title: make()
59.text: The make method creates a new collection instance from the given items. This is equivalent to calling new Collection or the collect helper. Collection.make1, 2, 3 //  Collection 1, 2, 3 From an object: Collection.make{ name: 'Taylor', role: 'admin' } //  Collection { name: 'Taylor', role: 'admin' } For wrapping non-collection values, use wrap. For creating an empty collection, use empty.

60.title: wrap()
60.text: The wrap method wraps the given value in a collection when applicable. Arrays and iterables are converted directly, single values become a one-element collection, and existing collections pass through unchanged. For an array: Collection.wrap1, 2, 3 //  Collection 1, 2, 3 For a single value: Collection.wrap'hello' //  Collection 'hello' An existing collection passes through unchanged: Collection.wrapcollect1, 2 //  Collection 1, 2 For extracting the underlying array, use unwrap. For creating fro

61.title: unwrap()
61.text: The unwrap method returns the underlying array from the given value when possible. If the value is already an array, it is returned as-is. If the value is a collection, the underlying array is extracted. To unwrap a collection: Collection.unwrapcollect1, 2, 3 //  1, 2, 3 If already an array, it passes through: Collection.unwrap1, 2, 3 //  1, 2, 3 For wrapping a value in a collection, use wrap. For getting items from an instance, use all.

62.title: empty()
62.text: The empty method creates an empty collection. This is useful when you need a typed empty collection as a starting point for building up items. Collection.empty //  Collection For a typed empty collection: Collection.empty<User> //  Collection<User> For creating with items, use make. For checking if a collection is empty, use isEmpty.

63.title: fromJson()
63.text: The fromJson method creates a collection from a JSON string. The string must be valid JSON representing either an array or an object. From JSON array: Collection.fromJson'1, 2, 3' //  Collection 1, 2, 3 From JSON object: Collection.fromJson'{"a": 1, "b": 2}' //  Collection {a: 1, b: 2} For converting collection to JSON, use toJson.

64.title: filter()
64.text: The filter method filters the collection using the given callback, keeping only items that pass a given truth test. If no callback is supplied, all falsy values false, null, undefined, 0, '' are removed. collect1, 2, 3, 4 .filtern => n > 2 //  3, 4 To remove falsy values, call without arguments: collect0, 1, '', 'hello', null .filter //  1, 'hello' For the inverse keeps items that fail, use reject. For Filter by key/value instead of callback, use where.

65.title: reject()
65.text: The reject method filters the collection using the given callback, removing items that pass the truth test. It is the inverse of the filter method. collect1, 2, 3, 4 .rejectn => n > 2 //  1, 2 You may also pass a value directly to reject by loose equality: collect1, null, 3 .rejectnull //  1, 3 For the inverse keeps items that pass, use filter. For excluding items in an array, use whereNotIn.

66.title: contains()
66.text: The contains method determines whether the collection contains a given item. Uses loose equality == to match Laravel behavior. Note that JS differs from PHP: 0 == false, null == undefined, "" == 0. collect1, 2, 3 .contains2 //  true You may pass a callback to check for a matching item: collect { name: 'Taylor', active: true }, { name: 'Abigail', active: false }, .containsu => u.active //  true You may also use key/value syntax: collect { name: 'Taylor', role: 'admin' }, { name: 'Abigail', role:

67.title: duplicates()
67.text: The duplicates method retrieves and returns duplicate values from the collection. By default, the method uses loose comparison. collect1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3 .duplicates //  2, 3, 3 You may also pass a key to compare by a derived value: collect{ email: 'a@b.com' }, { email: 'c@d.com' }, { email: 'a@b.com' } .duplicates'email' //  { email: 'a@b.com' } For strict equality ===, use duplicatesStrict. For get unique items instead, use unique.

68.title: duplicatesStrict()
68.text: The duplicatesStrict method retrieves duplicate values using strict equality ===. For loose equality ==, use duplicates.

69.title: except()
69.text: The except method returns all items in the collection except for those with the specified keys. collect{ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 } .except'a', 'c' //  Collection { b: 2 } For Include only specified keys, use only. For Filter by custom callback, use filter.

70.title: only()
70.text: The only method returns the items in the collection with the specified keys. collect{ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 } .only'a', 'c' //  Collection { a: 1, c: 3 } For Exclude specified keys, use except. For Pick specific properties from each item, use select.

71.title: skip()
71.text: The skip method returns a new collection without the first N items. collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5 .skip2 //  3, 4, 5 For Take the first N items, use take. For Skip and take in one call, use slice.

72.title: skipUntil()
72.text: The skipUntil method skips items until the given callback returns true. The matching item and all remaining items are returned as a new collection. You may also pass a value instead of a callback. collect1, 2, 3, 4 .skipUntilnumber => number >= 3 //  3, 4 You may also pass a value: collect'a', 'b', 'c', 'd' .skipUntil'c' //  'c', 'd' For Skip while condition is true, use skipWhile. For Take items until condition is met, use takeUntil.

73.title: skipWhile()
73.text: The skipWhile method skips items while the given callback returns true. Once the callback returns false, all remaining items are returned as a new collection. collect1, 1, 2, 3, 1 .skipWhilenumber => number < 2 //  2, 3, 1 For Skip until condition becomes true, use skipUntil. For Take while condition is true, use takeWhile.

74.title: take()
74.text: The take method returns a new collection with the specified number of items. You may pass a negative integer to take that many items from the end of the collection. collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5 .take3 //  1, 2, 3 With negative values, it takes from the end: collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5 .take-2 //  4, 5 For Skip the first N items, use skip. For Skip and take in one call, use slice.

75.title: takeUntil()
75.text: The takeUntil method returns items until the given callback returns true. The item that matches is not included in the result. You may also pass a value instead of a callback. collect1, 2, 3, 4 .takeUntilnumber => number >= 3 //  1, 2 You may also pass a value: collect'a', 'b', 'c', 'd' .takeUntil'c' //  'a', 'b' For Take while condition is true, use takeWhile. For Skip items until condition is met, use skipUntil.

76.title: takeWhile()
76.text: The takeWhile method returns items while the given callback returns true. Once the callback returns false, the method stops and returns what it collected so far. collect1, 2, 3, 4 .takeWhilenumber => number < 3 //  1, 2 For Take until condition becomes true, use takeUntil. For Skip while condition is true, use skipWhile.

77.title: nth()
77.text: The nth method creates a new collection containing every n-th element. You may optionally pass an offset as the second argument. collect'a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f' .nth2 //  'a', 'c', 'e' You may also pass an offset: collect'a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f' .nth2, 1 //  'b', 'd', 'f' For filtering with a custom callback, use filter.

78.title: unique()
78.text: The unique method returns all of the unique items in the collection. When dealing with nested objects, you may specify a key used to determine uniqueness. collect1, 1, 2, 2, 3 .unique //  Collection 1, 2, 3 By property: collect { id: 1, email: 'taylor@example.com' }, { id: 2, email: 'abigail@example.com' }, { id: 3, email: 'taylor@example.com' }, .unique'email' // //     { id: 1, email: 'taylor@example.com' }, //     { id: 2, email: 'abigail@example.com' }, // For strict equality always, use un

79.title: uniqueStrict()
79.text: The uniqueStrict method removes duplicate items using strict equality ===. Unlike unique, which uses loose comparison, this method distinguishes between values like 1 and '1'. collect1, '1', 2, '2', 2 .uniqueStrict //  1, '1', 2, '2' For loose equality, use unique. For Get duplicates using strict equality, use duplicatesStrict.

80.title: where()
80.text: The where method filters the collection by a given key/value pair. The method uses "loose" comparisons when checking item values, meaning a string with an integer value will be considered equal to an integer of the same value. Use the whereStrict method for strict comparisons. You may optionally pass a comparison operator as the second argument. Supported operators: =, ==, !=, <>, <, >, <=, >=. collect { product: 'Desk', price: 200 }, { product: 'Chair', price: 100 }, { product: 'Bookcase', pri

81.title: whereStrict()
81.text: The whereStrict method filters the collection by a given key/value pair using strict comparison ===. Unlike where, this method distinguishes between values like 1 and '1'. For loose equality, use where.

82.title: whereIn()
82.text: The whereIn method filters the collection by a given key/value contained within the given array. collect { name: 'Taylor', role: 'admin' }, { name: 'Abigail', role: 'editor' }, { name: 'James', role: 'user' }, .whereIn'role', 'admin', 'editor' // //     { name: 'Taylor', role: 'admin' }, //     { name: 'Abigail', role: 'editor' }, // For excluding items in an array, use whereNotIn. For Match single value, use where.

83.title: whereInStrict()
83.text: The whereInStrict method filters the collection by a given key/value contained within the given array using strict comparison ===. Unlike whereIn, this method distinguishes between values like 1 and '1'. collect{ id: 1 }, { id: '1' }, { id: 2 } .whereInStrict'id', 1 //  { id: 1 } For loose equality, use whereIn. For Exclude using strict equality, use whereNotInStrict.

84.title: whereNotIn()
84.text: The whereNotIn method filters the collection by a given key/value not contained within the given array. collect { name: 'Taylor', status: 'active' }, { name: 'Abigail', status: 'banned' }, { name: 'James', status: 'active' }, .whereNotIn'status', 'banned', 'suspended' // //     { name: 'Taylor', status: 'active' }, //     { name: 'James', status: 'active' }, // For Include items matching array, use whereIn. For Exclude by callback, use reject.

85.title: whereNotInStrict()
85.text: The whereNotInStrict method filters the collection by a given key/value not contained within the given array using strict comparison ===. Unlike whereNotIn, this method distinguishes between values like 1 and '1'. collect{ id: 1 }, { id: '1' }, { id: 2 } .whereNotInStrict'id', 1 //  { id: '1' }, { id: 2 } For loose equality, use whereNotIn. For Include using strict equality, use whereInStrict.

86.title: whereBetween()
86.text: The whereBetween method filters the collection by determining if a specified item value is within a given range. collect { name: 'Chair', price: 100 }, { name: 'Desk', price: 200 }, { name: 'Lamp', price: 30 }, .whereBetween'price', 50, 150 //  { name: 'Chair', price: 100 } For excluding items outside a range, use whereNotBetween. For Filter with operators, use where.

87.title: whereNotBetween()
87.text: The whereNotBetween method filters the collection by determining if a specified item value is outside of a given range. For Include items in range, use whereBetween.

88.title: whereNull()
88.text: The whereNull method filters the collection by determining if a specified item value is null or undefined. collect { name: 'Taylor', email: 'taylor@example.com' }, { name: 'Abigail', email: null }, .whereNull'email' //  { name: 'Abigail', email: null } For Exclude null/undefined values, use whereNotNull.

89.title: whereNotNull()
89.text: The whereNotNull method filters the collection by determining if a specified item value is not null or undefined. collect { name: 'Taylor', verifiedAt: '2024-01-15' }, { name: 'Abigail', verifiedAt: null }, .whereNotNull'verifiedAt' //  { name: 'Taylor', verifiedAt: '2024-01-15' } For Include null/undefined values, use whereNull.

90.title: whereInstanceOf()
90.text: The whereInstanceOf method filters the collection by a given class type, keeping only items that are instances of the specified class. This is useful for filtering mixed collections to a specific type. class User {} class Admin extends User {} collectnew User, new Admin, { name: 'plain' } .whereInstanceOfUser //  User, Admin For filtering with a custom callback, use filter.

91.title: forPage()
91.text: The forPage method returns a new collection containing the items that would be present on a given page number. The method accepts the page number as its first argument and the number of items to show per page as its second argument. collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 .forPage2, 3 //  4, 5, 6 For the first page: collect'a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e' .forPage1, 2 //  'a', 'b' For Get items by offset and length, use slice. For Take the first N items, use take.

92.title: all()
92.text: The all method returns the underlying array or object represented by the collection. Array-backed collections return an array, while associative collections return a plain object. For an array collection: collect1, 2, 3.all //  1, 2, 3 For an associative collection: collect{ name: 'Taylor', role: 'admin' }.all //  { name: 'Taylor', role: 'admin' } For always getting an array, use toArray. For Static version, use unwrap.

93.title: get()
93.text: The get method returns the item at a given key. If the key does not exist, undefined is returned. You may optionally pass a default value as the second argument, or a callback that returns the default. collect{ name: 'Taylor', role: 'admin' }.get'name' //  'Taylor' You may pass a default value: collect{ name: 'Taylor' }.get'role', 'guest' //  'guest' Or pass a callback that returns the default: collect{ name: 'Taylor' }.get'role',  => computeDefault //  result of computeDefault For Get or store

94.title: getOrPut()
94.text: The getOrPut method retrieves an item by key. If the key does not exist, the default value is stored in the collection and returned. This is useful for lazily populating collection values. const data = collect{ a: 1 } data.getOrPut'b', 2 //  2 data.all //  { a: 1, b: 2 } You may also pass a factory function: data.getOrPut'expensive',  => computeExpensiveValue //  computed value only computed if key missing For Get without storing a default, use get. For Store a value at a key, use put.

95.title: first()
95.text: The first method returns the first element in the collection that passes a given truth test. You may also call the method with no arguments to get the first element. If the collection is empty, the default value or undefined is returned. collect1, 2, 3 .first //  1 You may also pass a callback: collect1, 2, 3, 4 .firstn => n > 2 //  3 You may also pass a default: collect .firstnull, 'default' //  'default' For Get the last item instead, use last. For throwing when no item found, use firstOrFail

96.title: last()
96.text: The last method returns the last element in the collection that passes a given truth test. You may also call the method with no arguments to get the last element. If the collection is empty, the default value or undefined is returned. collect1, 2, 3 .last //  3 You may also pass a callback: collect1, 2, 3, 4 .lastn => n < 3 //  2 For Get the first item instead, use first. For Remove and return the last item, use pop.

97.title: keys()
97.text: The keys method returns all of the collection's keys as a new collection. For array-backed collections, this returns the numeric indices as strings. For an associative collection: collect{ a: 1, b: 2 }.keys //  Collection 'a', 'b' For an array collection: collect10, 20, 30.keys //  Collection '0', '1', '2' For Get all values, use values. For Check if a key exists, use has.

98.title: values()
98.text: The values method returns all of the collection's values as a new collection with reset, sequential integer keys. For an associative collection: collect{ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }.values //  Collection 1, 2, 3 To reset keys after filtering: collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5 .filtern => n > 2 .values //  Collection 3, 4, 5 with keys 0, 1, 2 For Get all keys, use keys. For Get the raw underlying data, use all.

99.title: slice()
99.text: The slice method returns a slice of the collection starting at the given index. You may pass a second argument to limit the size of the returned slice. collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5.slice2 //  Collection 3, 4, 5 You may also pass a length limit: collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5.slice1, 2 //  Collection 2, 3 With a negative offset, it counts from the end: collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5.slice-2 //  Collection 4, 5 For Take items from beginning or end, use take. For Skip items from the beginning, use skip.

100.title: pull()
100.text: The pull method removes and returns an item from the collection by its key. If the key does not exist, the default value is returned. This method mutates the collection. const data = collect{ name: 'Taylor', role: 'admin' } data.pull'name' //  'Taylor' data.all //  { role: 'admin' } You may pass a default value: collect{ a: 1 }.pull'missing', 'default' //  'default' For Get without removing, use get. For Remove and return the last item, use pop.

101.title: pop()
101.text: The pop method removes and returns the last item from the collection. You may pass a count to remove and return multiple items from the end. If the collection is empty, null is returned. For a single item: const data = collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5 data.pop //  5 data.all //  1, 2, 3, 4 For multiple items: collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5.pop2 //  Collection 4, 5 For an empty collection: collect.pop //  null For Remove from the beginning, use shift. For Remove by key, use pull.

102.title: shift()
102.text: The shift method removes and returns the first item from the collection. You may pass a count to remove and return multiple items from the beginning. If the collection is empty, null is returned. For a single item: const data = collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5 data.shift //  1 data.all //  2, 3, 4, 5 For multiple items: collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5.shift2 //  Collection 1, 2 For an empty collection: collect.shift //  null For Remove from the end, use pop. For Remove by key, use pull.

103.title: select()
103.text: The select method selects the given keys from each item in the collection, similar to a SQL SELECT statement. This is useful for extracting only the properties you need from complex objects. const users = collect { id: 1, name: 'Taylor', email: 'taylor@example.com', role: 'admin' }, { id: 2, name: 'Abigail', email: 'abigail@example.com', role: 'user' } users.select'name', 'email' //  Collection { name: 'Taylor', email: '...' }, { name: 'Abigail', email: '...' } For nested properties: collect{ u

104.title: search()
104.text: The search method searches the collection for the given value and returns its key if found. If the item is not found, false is returned. By default, comparison uses loose equality. Pass true as the second argument for strict comparison. collect2, 4, 6, 8.search4 //  '1' You may also pass a callback: collect2, 4, 6, 8.searchitem => item > 5 //  '2' For strict comparison: collect2, 4, '6', 8.search'6', true //  '2' For Check if a value exists, use contains. For Get the first matching item, use fi

105.title: sole()
105.text: The sole method returns the first element in the collection that passes a given truth test, but only if the truth test matches exactly one element. collect1, 2, 3, 4 .solen => n === 2 //  2 You may also use key/value syntax: collect{ id: 1, active: true }, { id: 2, active: false } .sole'active', true //  { id: 1, active: true } For Get first matching item without throwing, use first. For Check without throwing, use hasSole.

106.title: firstOrFail()
106.text: The firstOrFail method returns the first element in the collection, or throws an ItemNotFoundException if the collection is empty or no matching element is found. collect1, 2, 3 .firstOrFailn => n > 2 //  3 You may also use key/value syntax: collect{ id: 1 }, { id: 2 } .firstOrFail'id', 2 //  { id: 2 } For Get first matching item without throwing, use first. For Get item only if exactly one matches, use sole.

107.title: random()
107.text: The random method returns a random item from the collection. You may optionally pass an integer to specify how many items you would like to retrieve. If the collection is empty, an exception is thrown. collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5.random //  3 random For multiple random items: collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5.random2 //  Collection 4, 1 random You may also pass a callback for count: collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5.randomitems => items.count - 2 //  Collection of 3 random items For Randomize the entire collection, use shuffle

108.title: firstWhere()
108.text: The firstWhere method returns the first element in the collection with the given key/value pair. collect { id: 1, name: 'Taylor', role: 'admin' }, { id: 2, name: 'Abigail', role: 'editor' }, .firstWhere'role', 'admin' //  { id: 1, name: 'Taylor', role: 'admin' } You may also pass a comparison operator: collect { id: 1, total: 50 }, { id: 2, total: 150 }, .firstWhere'total', '>', 100 //  { id: 2, total: 150 }

109.title: value()
109.text: The value method retrieves a given value from the first element of the collection. This is useful for quickly extracting a single property from the first item without having to call first separately. collect { name: 'Taylor', role: 'admin' }, { name: 'Abigail', role: 'user' } .value'name' //  'Taylor' You may pass a default: collect.value'name', 'Unknown' //  'Unknown' For Get the first item, use first. For Extract a property from all items, use pluck.

110.title: offsetGet()
110.text: Get the value at a given offset. Part of the ArrayAccess interface for bracket-style access. Unlike get, this method does not support default values and returns undefined for missing keys. collect{ name: 'Taylor', role: 'Developer' } .offsetGet'name' //  'Taylor' For Primary method with default value support, use get. For Check if key exists, use offsetExists.

111.title: chunk()
111.text: Split the collection into chunks of the given size. collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5 .chunk2 // //   Collection 1, 2, //   Collection 3, 4, //   Collection 5, // For Split into N groups, use split. For Create overlapping windows, use sliding.

112.title: chunkWhile()
112.text: The chunkWhile method breaks the collection into multiple, smaller collections based on the evaluation of the given callback. The callback receives the current item, its key, and the current chunk being built. A new chunk starts whenever the callback returns false. To group consecutive numbers: collect1, 2, 3, 5, 6 .chunkWhilev, k, chunk => v === chunk.last + 1 // //   1, 2, 3, //   5, 6, // For Split into fixed-size chunks, use chunk. For Split into a specific number of groups, use split.

113.title: split()
113.text: The split method breaks a collection into the given number of groups, distributing extra items across earlier groups to balance sizes as evenly as possible. To split into three groups: collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5 .split3 // //   1, 2, //   3, 4, //   5, // For Fill non-terminal groups completely first, use splitIn. For Split into fixed-size chunks instead, use chunk.

114.title: splitIn()
114.text: The splitIn method breaks a collection into the given number of groups, filling non-terminal groups completely before allocating the remainder to the final group. Unlike split, which balances group sizes, splitIn creates full-sized chunks until items run out. To split into three groups: collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 .splitIn3 // //   1, 2, 3, //   4, 5, 6, //   7, // For Distribute items evenly across groups, use split. For Split into fixed-size chunks, use chunk.

115.title: countBy()
115.text: The countBy method counts the occurrences of values in the collection. By default it counts by the value itself, but you can pass a callback or property key to count by a derived grouping key. collect1, 2, 2, 3 .countBy //  {'1': 1, '2': 2, '3': 1} To count by email domain: collect'alice@gmail.com', 'bob@yahoo.com', 'carlos@gmail.com' .countByemail => email.split'@'1 //  {'gmail.com': 2, 'yahoo.com': 1} For Group items instead of counting them, use groupBy. For Get total item count, use count.

116.title: groupBy()
116.text: Group items by a key or callback result. By property: collect { name: 'Taylor', role: 'admin' }, { name: 'Abigail', role: 'editor' }, { name: 'James', role: 'editor' }, .groupBy'role' //  { //     admin: { name: 'Taylor', role: 'admin' }, //     editor: //       { name: 'Abigail', role: 'editor' }, //       { name: 'James', role: 'editor' }, //     , //   } You may also pass a callback: collect { id: 1, total: 150 }, { id: 2, total: 50 }, { id: 3, total: 200 }, .groupByo => o.total > 100 ? 'lar

117.title: keyBy()
117.text: Key the collection by a field or callback result. If multiple items have the same key, only the last one is kept. collect { id: 1, name: 'Taylor' }, { id: 2, name: 'Abigail' }, .keyBy'id' //  { //     1: { id: 1, name: 'Taylor' }, //     2: { id: 2, name: 'Abigail' }, //   } For Similar but keeps all items per key, use groupBy. For Transform and key in one step, use mapWithKeys.

118.title: partition()
118.text: Split the collection into two groups: items passing the test and items failing. const active, inactive = collect { name: 'Taylor', active: true }, { name: 'Abigail', active: false }, { name: 'James', active: true }, .partitionu => u.active // active   { name: 'Taylor', ... }, { name: 'James', ... } // inactive  { name: 'Abigail', ... } You may also use key/value syntax: const admins, others = collect { name: 'Taylor', role: 'admin' }, { name: 'Abigail', role: 'editor' }, .partition'role', 'admi

119.title: sliding()
119.text: The sliding method returns a new collection of chunks representing a "sliding window" view of the items. Each chunk contains size consecutive items, and the window advances by step items between chunks. For pairs of consecutive items: collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5 .sliding2 //  1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5 For triplets with a step of 2: collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 .sliding3, 2 //  1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5 For Non-overlapping fixed-size chunks, use chunk. For Conditional chunking, use chunkWhile.

120.text: The Collection class provides a fluent, convenient wrapper for working with arrays of data. For example, check out the following code. We'll use the collect helper to create a new collection instance from the array, convert each element to uppercase, and then remove all empty elements: const collection = collect'Taylor', 'Abigail', null .mapname => name?.toUpperCase .rejectname => !name; As you can see, the Collection class allows you to chain its methods to perform fluent mapping and reducing

121.title: Creating Collections
121.text: As mentioned above, the collect helper returns a new Collection instance for the given array. So, creating a collection is as simple as: const collection = collect1, 2, 3; You may also create a collection using the make and fromJson methods.

122.title: Extending Collections
122.text: Collections are "macroable", which allows you to add additional methods to the Collection class at runtime. The Collection.macro static method accepts a name and a function that will be executed when your macro is called. The macro function may access the collection's methods via this, just as if it were a real method of the collection class. For example, the following code adds a toUpper method to the Collection class: import { Collection, collect } from 'collect-ts'; Collection.macro'toUpper'

123.text: For the majority of the remaining collection documentation, we'll discuss each method available on the Collection class. Remember, all of these methods may be chained to fluently manipulate the underlying array. 124.text: after {.collection-method .first-collection-method} The after method returns the item after the given item. null is returned if the given item is not found or is the last item: collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5.after3; collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5.after5; The first call returns 4, and the second returns null since 5 is the last item. After that time, the collection will then stop enumerating: const lazyCollection = LazyCollection.timesInfinity .takeUntilTimeoutnew DateDate.now + 60000; lazyCollection.eachnumber => { conso

131.title: reverse()
131.text: The reverse method reverses the order of the collection's items, preserving the original keys. collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5 .reverse //  5, 4, 3, 2, 1 For Sort items, use sort. For Sort in descending order, use sortDesc.

132.title: shuffle()
132.text: The shuffle method randomly shuffles the items in the collection. Uses the Fisher-Yates algorithm for unbiased shuffling. collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5 .shuffle //  3, 1, 4, 5, 2 random order For Get random items, use random. For Sort items, use sort.

133.title: sort()
133.text: The sort method sorts the collection. The sorted collection keeps the original keys, but the order of items changes. You may pass a custom comparison callback for more control over sorting behavior. collect5, 3, 1, 2, 4 .sort //  1, 2, 3, 4, 5 You may pass a custom comparator: collect { name: 'Taylor', age: 32 }, { name: 'Abigail', age: 28 }, .sorta, b => a.age - b.age // //     { name: 'Abigail', age: 28 }, //     { name: 'Taylor', age: 32 }, // For Sort in descending order, use sortDesc. For

134.title: sortDesc()
134.text: The sortDesc method sorts the collection in the opposite order as the sort method. collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5 .sortDesc //  5, 4, 3, 2, 1 For Sort in ascending order, use sort. For Sort by property in descending order, use sortByDesc.

135.title: sortBy()
135.text: The sortBy method sorts the collection by the given key. The sorted collection keeps the original array keys, so in the following example we will use the values method to reset the keys to consecutively numbered indexes. collect { name: 'Taylor', age: 32 }, { name: 'Abigail', age: 28 }, .sortBy'name' // //     { name: 'Abigail', age: 28 }, //     { name: 'Taylor', age: 32 }, // You may also pass a callback: collect { name: 'Taylor', age: 32 }, { name: 'Abigail', age: 28 }, .sortByu => u.age //

136.title: sortByDesc()
136.text: The sortByDesc method sorts the collection in the opposite order as the sortBy method. This method has the same signature as sortBy, but will sort in descending order. collect { name: 'Taylor', age: 32 }, { name: 'Abigail', age: 28 }, .sortByDesc'age' // //     { name: 'Taylor', age: 32 }, //     { name: 'Abigail', age: 28 }, // You may also pass a callback: collect { name: 'Chair', price: 100 }, { name: 'Desk', price: 200 }, .sortByDescp => p.price // //     { name: 'Desk', price: 200 }, //

137.title: sortKeys()
137.text: The sortKeys method sorts the collection by the keys of the underlying associative array. Uses locale-aware string comparison for key ordering. collect{ b: 2, a: 1, c: 3 } .sortKeys //  { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 } For Sort keys in descending order, use sortKeysDesc. For Sort keys with custom callback, use sortKeysUsing.

138.title: sortKeysDesc()
138.text: The sortKeysDesc method sorts the collection by the keys in descending order. collect{ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 } .sortKeysDesc //  { c: 3, b: 2, a: 1 } For Sort keys in ascending order, use sortKeys. For Sort keys with custom callback, use sortKeysUsing.

139.title: sortKeysUsing()
139.text: The sortKeysUsing method sorts the collection by its keys using a callback. The callback must be a comparison function returning a negative integer, zero, or a positive integer to indicate sort order. For natural sorting: collect{ 'item2': 'b', 'item10': 'c', 'item1': 'a' } .sortKeysUsinga, b => a.localeCompareb, undefined, { numeric: true } //  { item1: 'a', item2: 'b', item10: 'c' } For Sort keys alphabetically, use sortKeys. For Sort keys in descending order, use sortKeysDesc.

140.title: range()
140.text: The range method creates a collection containing numbers within a specified range. Works in both directions: ascending when from < to, descending otherwise. In ascending order: Collection.range1, 5 //  Collection 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 In descending order: Collection.range5, 1 //  Collection 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 For Generate by calling a function N times, use times.

141.title: times()
141.text: The times method creates a new collection by invoking the given closure a specified number of times. The callback receives 1-based indices 1, 2, 3.... Without a callback, returns a collection of numbers 1 through N. You may also pass a callback: Collection.times3, i => i  2 //  Collection 2, 4, 6 Without a callback, it returns numbers 1 through N: Collection.times3 //  Collection 1, 2, 3 For Generate a range between two numbers, use range.

142.title: map()
142.text: The map method iterates over the collection and passes each value to the given callback. The callback is free to modify the item and return it, thus forming a new collection of modified items. collect1, 2, 3 .mapn => n  2 //  Collection 2, 4, 6 To extract a property: collect { name: 'Taylor' }, { name: 'Abigail' }, .mapu => u.name //  'Taylor', 'Abigail' For Extract a single property by key, use pluck. For Transform and change keys, use mapWithKeys.

143.title: mapWithKeys()
143.text: The mapWithKeys method iterates through the collection and passes each value to the given callback. The callback should return an associative array containing a single key/value pair. collect { name: 'John', department: 'Sales' }, { name: 'Jane', department: 'Marketing' } .mapWithKeysemp => emp.name, emp.department //  { John: 'Sales', Jane: 'Marketing' } For Transform values keeping original keys, use map. For Key by a property without transforming values, use keyBy.

144.title: mapToDictionary()
144.text: The mapToDictionary method runs the given callback over each item and groups the returned values by their keys. Unlike groupBy, this method allows complete control over the grouped values through the callback's return tuple. collect { name: 'John', department: 'Sales' }, { name: 'Jane', department: 'Sales' }, { name: 'Bob', department: 'Marketing' } .mapToDictionaryemp => emp.department, emp.name //  { Sales: 'John', 'Jane', Marketing: 'Bob' } For Similar but returns nested Collections, use map

145.title: mapToGroups()
145.text: The mapToGroups method groups the collection's items by the given callback. The callback should return an associative array containing a single key/value pair, allowing you to customize both the group key and the value placed in each group. collect { name: 'John', department: 'Sales' }, { name: 'Jane', department: 'Sales' }, { name: 'Bob', department: 'Marketing' } .mapToGroupsemp => emp.department, emp.name //  { Sales: Collection'John', 'Jane', Marketing: Collection'Bob' } For Similar but ret

146.title: mapInto()
146.text: The mapInto method iterates over the collection and creates a new instance of the given class for each item, passing the item value and key to the constructor. class Currency { constructorpublic amount: number {} format { return $${this.amount.toFixed2}; } } collect100, 250, 50 .mapIntoCurrency .mapc => c.format //  '$100.00', '$250.00', '$50.00' For Transform with arbitrary callback, use map. For passing entire collection to a class constructor, use pipeInto.

147.title: mapSpread()
147.text: The mapSpread method iterates over the collection's items, passing each nested item value into the given callback as separate arguments. This is useful when working with nested arrays where each sub-array's elements should be passed as individual arguments. collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 .mapSpreada, b => a + b //  3, 7, 11 You may also pass a key as the final argument: collect'Taylor', 'Laravel', 'Caleb', 'Livewire' .mapSpreadname, project, key => ${key}: ${name} - ${project} //  '0: Taylor - Laravel

148.title: flatMap()
148.text: Map each item then flatten the results by one level. collect1, 2, 3, 4 .flatMaparr => arr.mapn => n  2 //  Collection 2, 4, 6, 8 For Transform without flattening, use map. For Flatten without mapping, use flatten.

149.title: collapse()
149.text: The collapse method collapses a collection of arrays into a single, flat collection. It merges the elements of nested arrays or Collections into one level. collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5 .collapse //  1, 2, 3, 4, 5 You may also use nested Collections: collectcollect1, 2, collect3, 4 .collapse //  1, 2, 3, 4 For Recursively flatten to any depth, use flatten. For Map then collapse, use flatMap.

150.title: collapseWithKeys()
150.text: The collapseWithKeys method collapses a collection of objects into a single object, preserving the keys from each nested object. Later objects override earlier ones when keys conflict. collect{ name: 'John' }, { email: 'john@example.com' }, { role: 'admin' } .collapseWithKeys //  { name: 'John', email: 'john@example.com', role: 'admin' } With overlapping keys, later values override: collect{ a: 1 }, { a: 2, b: 3 } .collapseWithKeys //  { a: 2, b: 3 } For Collapse arrays into a flat array, use c

151.title: flatten()
151.text: The flatten method flattens a multi-dimensional collection into a single dimension. You may optionally pass a depth argument to limit how many levels deep the flattening should go. To flatten all levels: collect1, 2, 3, 4 .flatten //  1, 2, 3, 4 To flatten just one level: collect1, 2, 3 .flatten1 //  1, 2, 3 For Flatten by exactly one level, use collapse. For Flatten to dot notation keys, use dot.

152.title: flip()
152.text: The flip method swaps the collection's keys with their corresponding values. Values are converted to strings since object keys must be strings. collect{ name: 'taylor', framework: 'laravel' } .flip //  { taylor: 'name', laravel: 'framework' } For an array, keys become values: collect'a', 'b', 'c' .flip //  { a: '0', b: '1', c: '2' } For Get just the keys, use keys. For Get just the values, use values.

153.title: pad()
153.text: The pad method fills the array with the given value until the array reaches the specified size. This method behaves like PHP's arraypad function. To pad to the left, specify a negative size. No padding occurs if the absolute value of the given size is less than or equal to the length of the array. To pad to the right: collect1, 2, 3 .pad5, 0 //  1, 2, 3, 0, 0 To pad to the left: collect1, 2, 3 .pad-5, 0 //  0, 0, 1, 2, 3 For Take items from start or end, use take. For Insert items at a position

154.title: forget()
154.text: The forget method removes an item from the collection by its key. Unlike except, this method modifies the collection in place. For numeric keys, the collection does not re-index the remaining items. To remove a single key: collect{ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 } .forget'b' //  Collection { a: 1, c: 3 } To remove multiple keys: collect{ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 } .forget'a', 'c' //  Collection { b: 2 } For returning new collection without specified keys, use except. For Remove and return a single value, use pull.

155.title: pluck()
155.text: Extract values at a given path from each item. collect { id: 1, name: 'Taylor' }, { id: 2, name: 'Abigail' }, .pluck'name' //  'Taylor', 'Abigail' You may also specify custom keys: collect { id: 1, name: 'Taylor' }, { id: 2, name: 'Abigail' }, .pluck'name', 'id' //  { 1: 'Taylor', 2: 'Abigail' } For Transform items with full callback control, use map. For Get first item's value at path, use value.

156.title: transform()
156.text: The transform method iterates over the collection and calls the given callback with each item in the collection. The items in the collection will be replaced by the values returned by the callback. Unlike map, this method modifies the collection in place. const collection = collect1, 2, 3; collection.transformn => n  2; collection.all; //  2, 4, 6 You may chain after transform: collect{ price: 100, tax: 10 } .transformv, k => k === 'price' ? v  1.1 : v .sum //  120 For Transform without mutatio

157.title: splice()
157.text: The splice method removes and returns a slice of items starting at the specified index. You may pass a second argument to limit the size of the removed slice, and a third argument containing replacement items to insert at the splice point. This method modifies the original collection. To remove from an index: const collection = collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5; const chunk = collection.splice2; // chunk       3, 4, 5 // collection  1, 2 To remove a specific length: const collection = collect1, 2, 3, 4, 5;

158.title: dot()
158.text: The dot method flattens a multi-dimensional collection into a single level collection that uses "dot" notation to indicate depth. This is useful for working with nested configuration or form data. collect{ user: { name: 'John', address: { city: 'NYC' } } }.dot //  { 'user.name': 'John', 'user.address.city': 'NYC' } To flatten configuration: collect{ database: { host: 'localhost', port: 3306 }, cache: { driver: 'redis' } }.dot //  { 'database.host': 'localhost', 'database.port': 3306, 'cache.dri

159.title: undot()
159.text: The undot method expands a single-level collection that uses "dot" notation into a multi-dimensional collection. This is the inverse of the dot method. collect{ 'user.name': 'John', 'user.address.city': 'NYC' }.undot //  { user: { name: 'John', address: { city: 'NYC' } } } To expand form data: collect{ 'items.0.name': 'Widget', 'items.0.price': 100, 'items.1.name': 'Gadget', 'items.1.price': 200 }.undot //  { items: { 0: { name: 'Widget', price: 100 }, 1: { name: 'Gadget', price: 200 } } } For

160.title: each()
160.text: The each method iterates over the items in the collection and passes each item to a closure. If you would like to stop iterating through the items, you may return false from your closure. collect1, 2, 3 .eachn => console.logn // logs: 1, 2, 3 To stop early: collect1, 2, 3 .eachn => { if n === 2 return false console .logn } // logs: 1 For Execute callback on entire collection, use tap. For Transform items instead of side effects, use map.

161.title: eachSpread()
161.text: The eachSpread method iterates over the collection's items, passing each nested item value into the given callback as separate arguments. This is useful when working with nested arrays where each sub-array should be destructured into callback parameters. collect'John', 35, 'Jane', 28 .eachSpreadname, age => { console.log${name} is ${age} years old; }; // Logs: "John is 35 years old" // Logs: "Jane is 28 years old" You may also pass a key as the final argument: collect'a', 'b', 'c', 'd' .eachSpr

162.title: collect()
162.text: The collect method returns a new Collection instance with the current items. This is useful when you want to break the chain and get a fresh collection, or convert a subclass back to a base Collection. const original = collect1, 2, 3; const copy = original.collect; // original and copy are separate instances For Convert subclass to base Collection, use toBase.

163.title: toBase()
163.text: The toBase method returns a base Collection instance from the current collection. This is useful when working with collection subclasses and you need to ensure you have a standard Collection instance. class CustomCollection extends Collection {} const custom = new CustomCollection1, 2, 3; const base = custom.toBase; // base instanceof Collection === true For Create a new collection copy, use collect.

164.title: pipe()
164.text: The pipe method passes the collection to the given closure and returns the result of the executed closure. This is useful for wrapping the collection in custom logic or breaking out of the method chain when needed. collect1, 2, 3 .pipec => c.sum  2 //  12 For conditional logic: collect { name: 'Taylor' }, { name: 'Abigail' }, { name: 'James' }, .pipec => c.isEmpty ? 'No users' : ${c.count} users //  '3 users' For Execute callback but return collection unchanged, use tap. For passing collection

165.title: pipeInto()
165.text: The pipeInto method creates a new instance of the given class and passes the collection into the constructor. This is useful for wrapping the collection in domain-specific objects or adapters. class Report { constructorprivate data: Collection<number> {} summary { return { total: this.data.sum, avg: this.data.avg }; } } collect10, 20, 30 .pipeIntoReport .summary //  { total: 60, avg: 20 } For passing collection to a callback, use pipe. For Create instances from each item, use mapInto.

166.title: pipeThrough()
166.text: The pipeThrough method passes the collection through a series of callbacks and returns the final result. Each callback receives the result of the previous callback, creating a pipeline of transformations. collect1, 2, 3 .pipeThrough c => c.sum,      // 6 n => n  2,        // 12 n => Total: ${n} // 'Total: 12' //  'Total: 12' For composable transformations: const addTax = c => c.mapp => p  1.1; const round = c => c.mapp => Math.roundp; collect100, 200 .pipeThroughaddTax, round .all //  110, 220

167.title: tap()
167.text: Pass the collection to the given callback and return it unchanged. Useful for debugging or side effects mid-chain. To debug mid-chain: collect1, 2, 3 .mapn => n  2 .tapc => console.logc.all .filtern => n > 2 For Execute callback for each item, use each. For Transform and return callback result, use pipe.

168.title: dump()
168.text: The dump method outputs the collection's items to the console and returns the collection, allowing you to inspect the contents at any point in a method chain without interrupting the flow. To debug mid-chain: collect1, 2, 3 .mapn => n  2 .dump              // Logs: 2, 4, 6 .filtern => n > 3 .all //  4, 6 You may also pass a label: collection.dump'after filter' // Logs: items... 'after filter' For Dump and halt execution, use dd. For Execute any callback mid-chain, use tap.

169.title: dd()
169.text: The dd method outputs the collection's items to the console and then throws an error to halt script execution. This is useful for debugging when you want to inspect the collection and stop processing. The name comes from "dump and die." collect1, 2, 3 .mapn => n  2 .dd  // Logs: 2, 4, 6, then throws .filtern => n > 3  // Never reached For Dump without halting, use dump.

170.title: when()
170.text: The when method will execute the given callback when the first argument given to the method evaluates to true. The collection instance and the resolved value are passed to the closure. An optional second callback is executed when the condition is falsy. collect1, 2, 3 .whenshouldDouble, c => c.mapn => n  2 .all You may pass a default callback: const filterActive = true collect { name: 'Desk', active: true }, { name: 'Chair', active: false }, .when filterActive, c => c.where'active', true, c =>

171.title: unless()
171.text: The unless method will execute the given callback when the first argument given to the method evaluates to false. This is the inverse of the when method. An optional second callback is executed when the condition is truthy. To skip filtering for admins: const isAdmin = false collect { title: 'Public Post', public: true }, { title: 'Draft', public: false }, .unlessisAdmin, c => c.where'public', true //  { title: 'Public Post', public: true } You may pass a default callback: const showAll = true

172.title: whenEmpty()
172.text: The whenEmpty method will execute the given callback when the collection is empty. An optional second callback is executed when the collection is not empty. To provide defaults for an empty collection: collect .whenEmptyc => collect'default' .all //  'default' To log empty state: collect .whenEmpty => console.log'No results found' // logs: 'No results found' For Execute when collection has items, use whenNotEmpty. For Execute on arbitrary condition, use when.

173.title: whenNotEmpty()
173.text: The whenNotEmpty method will execute the given callback when the collection is not empty. An optional second callback is executed when the collection is empty. To process only if items exist: collect { id: 1, total: 100 }, { id: 2, total: 200 }, .whenNotEmptyc => c.pluck'total' //  100, 200 You may pass an empty fallback: collect{ name: 'Taylor' } .whenNotEmpty c => c.first, => 'No results' //  { name: 'Taylor' } For Execute when collection is empty, use whenEmpty. For Execute on arbitrary cond

176.title: offsetSet()
176.text: Set the value at a given offset.

177.title: offsetUnset()
177.text: Remove the value at a given offset.

178.title: lazy()
178.text: The lazy method returns a new LazyCollection instance from the underlying items. This is particularly useful when you need to perform transformations on a large collection and want to defer processing until the items are actually needed.
